dct_description_sm: Northern regions are experiencing accelerated climate warming, driving permafrost thaw, shrubification, and projected increases in mercury (Hg) release to freshwater systems and exposure in fish. We aim to first, develop and validate the use of the delamination technique of fish eye lenses as historical archives of mercury (Hg) and selenium (Se) concentrations, and then, to apply this approach in Nunavik using the eye lenses of long-lived (10-40 years) lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush), a higher trophic-level species of significant cultural and dietary importance in Kangiqsualujjuaq, Nunavik. The fish eye lens grows concentrically throughout an individuals lifetime, analogous to tree ring growth, with each lamina preserving a physiological record of exposure to mercury and other contaminants. Using a delamination technique, Hg and Se concentrations can be measured at an annual resolution and related to fish age, allowing changes in exposure to be tracked over decades. For method development, we are applying delamination to eye lenses of lake whitefish (Coregonus clupeaformis) and northern pike (Esox lucius) sourced from existing projects. For the main objective, community-based sampling of lake trout is currently underway in Kangiqsualujjuaq (call-out period: 03-2026 to 07-2026). This work offers a novel biomonitoring tool for the reconstruction of historical Hg and Se exposure in Nunavik, without the need for extensive sampling programmes. Additionally, the research will provide relevant information on contaminant (Hg) and nutrient (Se) levels in important traditional food species. Linking eye lens data to permafrost data and traditional knowledge will further inform on environmental drivers of change in mercury exposure and dynamics across lakes impacted by climate change.

dct_title_s: Metal concentrations in fish eyes of Nunavik
